title: Allergic Rhinitis: Treat the Nose, Check the Asthma
bottomLine: Allergic rhinitis causes recurrent nasal itching, sneezing, watery rhinorrhea and congestion linked to allergen exposure. Intranasal corticosteroids are among the most effective treatments for persistent symptoms, and coexisting asthma should be actively assessed.
recognize: Allergic shiners, pale edematous mucosa and seasonal/perennial patterns can support the diagnosis.
differentiate: Viral rhinitis is acute and self-limited; bacterial sinusitis follows a different time course; unilateral obstruction/bleeding raises structural concern.
assessment: Ask triggers, seasonality, indoor exposures, asthma symptoms, sleep, occupational factors and medication use including decongestants.
workup: Allergy testing is useful when the diagnosis or trigger is unclear or when immunotherapy is being considered, not routinely for every typical case.
management: Use allergen reduction where practical, intranasal corticosteroid and/or second-generation antihistamine based on symptoms; consider immunotherapy for selected persistent disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid prolonged topical nasal decongestant use because of rhinitis medicamentosa; first-generation antihistamines cause sedation and anticholinergic effects.
counselling: Teach correct intranasal spray technique directed away from the septum.
followUp: Reassess adherence/technique and asthma before escalating therapy.
examTrap: Ordering a broad food allergy panel for isolated seasonal nasal symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Allergic rhinitis is an airway disease—ask about the lungs too.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology resources

title: Food Allergy: Reproducible Immediate Reaction, Not a Positive Panel Alone
bottomLine: IgE-mediated food allergy is diagnosed from a convincing reaction history supported by targeted testing. Positive skin or serum IgE without a compatible clinical reaction indicates sensitization, not necessarily clinical allergy.
recognize: Immediate hives, angioedema, wheeze, vomiting or hypotension after a specific food supports IgE-mediated disease.
differentiate: Food intolerance, celiac disease, lactose intolerance and non-IgE GI disorders have different mechanisms and testing.
assessment: Document exact food/form, dose, timing, symptoms, cofactors such as exercise/alcohol and subsequent tolerance.
workup: Use targeted skin-prick or specific IgE testing based on history; oral food challenge is the diagnostic gold standard when needed and must be done in an appropriate setting.
management: Avoid confirmed trigger, prescribe epinephrine auto-injector when anaphylaxis risk warrants and refer allergy for diagnosis, challenge or immunotherapy options.
medicationSafety: Do not use antihistamines as a substitute for epinephrine in anaphylaxis.
redFlags: Multiple food restriction with nutritional compromise
counselling: Teach label reading and individualized emergency plans without recommending unnecessary avoidance of unrelated foods.
followUp: Reassess childhood food allergies because some resolve and unnecessary lifelong restriction has harms.
examTrap: Diagnosing ten food allergies from a broad positive IgE panel in a patient who eats those foods without symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Sensitization is a test result; allergy is a clinical reaction.
sourceBasis: Canadian Society of Allergy and Clinical Immunology guidance

title: Hearing Loss: Conductive, Sensorineural, or Sudden Emergency?
bottomLine: Hearing loss is first classified as conductive versus sensorineural. Sudden unilateral sensorineural hearing loss developing over hours to a few days is an otologic emergency and should not be treated as wax or routine congestion without urgent assessment.
recognize: Cerumen, otitis media and tympanic membrane disease cause conductive loss; age, noise, ototoxic drugs and inner-ear disease cause sensorineural loss.
differentiate: Tuning-fork tests can help classify but do not replace audiometry; unilateral/asymmetric sensorineural loss warrants further evaluation.
assessment: Ask onset, laterality, tinnitus, vertigo, pain/discharge, noise, medications, neurologic symptoms and childhood speech/development.
workup: Inspect canal/TM and obtain audiometry; urgent audiology/ENT for sudden sensorineural loss, with imaging or other tests for asymmetric disease as indicated.
management: Remove obstructing wax when safe, treat middle-ear disease and urgently treat sudden sensorineural loss according to ENT pathway; provide hearing aids or assistive communication for chronic loss.
medicationSafety: Aminoglycosides and selected chemotherapy/loop diuretic exposures can be ototoxic; review cumulative exposure.
counselling: Hearing loss can worsen cognition and social isolation; offer communication strategies and rehabilitation.
followUp: Track asymmetric or progressive loss and hearing-aid benefit.
examTrap: Telling a patient with sudden unilateral hearing loss to try decongestants for a week before audiology.
oneLinePearl: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is time-sensitive.
sourceBasis: Canadian otolaryngology and audiology practice principles

title: Tinnitus: Pulsatile, Unilateral, or Neurologic Changes the Workup
bottomLine: Most nonpulsatile bilateral tinnitus is associated with hearing loss and managed with hearing assessment, reassurance and symptom strategies. Pulsatile, unilateral/asymmetric or neurologically associated tinnitus needs targeted investigation.
recognize: Noise exposure, age-related hearing loss, medications and TMJ disorders can contribute.
differentiate: Pulsatile tinnitus can reflect vascular pathology and is not managed like ordinary subjective ringing.
assessment: Ask pulsatile versus nonpulsatile, laterality, hearing loss, vertigo, neurologic symptoms, medication/noise exposure and distress/sleep impact.
workup: Perform otoscopy and audiometry; vascular or neuroimaging is selected for pulsatile/asymmetric/red-flag patterns.
management: Treat reversible cause, hearing loss and distress; CBT/sound strategies can reduce burden even when the signal persists.
medicationSafety: Review ototoxic medications rather than promising that stopping every suspected drug will reverse chronic tinnitus.
counselling: Assess severe distress and suicidality in disabling tinnitus.
followUp: Refer persistent asymmetric or pulsatile cases appropriately.
examTrap: Reassuring unilateral pulsatile tinnitus as ordinary age-related hearing change without vascular evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Pulsatile tinnitus is a vascular question until evaluated.
sourceBasis: Canadian ENT and audiology practice resources

title: Dental Infection: Antibiotics Do Not Replace Dental Source Control
bottomLine: Localized odontogenic infection requires dental treatment of the diseased tooth or drainage; antibiotics are reserved for spreading infection, systemic involvement or selected high-risk contexts. Facial swelling with airway or deep-space signs is an emergency.
recognize: Tooth pain, percussion tenderness, gingival swelling and fluctuance support an odontogenic source.
differentiate: Sinusitis, TMJ pain, trigeminal neuralgia and salivary disease can mimic dental pain.
assessment: Assess facial/neck swelling, fever, trismus, floor-of-mouth elevation, swallowing/breathing, immune status and dental access.
workup: Dental imaging is selected by dental/acute care; CT neck is indicated when deep-space infection is suspected.
management: Provide analgesia and urgent dental source control; use antibiotics for systemic or spreading infection and transfer Ludwig angina/airway risk emergently.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated antibiotic courses for untreated tooth infection; NSAID/acetaminophen analgesia is often more effective than opioids for dental pain when safe.
counselling: Explain that dental infection recurs until the tooth/source is definitively treated.
followUp: Ensure the patient can access dental care, including public/community resources when cost is a barrier.
examTrap: Prescribing a third antibiotic course for the same dental abscess without arranging source control.
oneLinePearl: Dental pus still needs dental treatment.
sourceBasis: Canadian dental and antimicrobial stewardship principles

title: Oral Lesions: Ulcer, Thrush, Leukoplakia, or Cancer?
bottomLine: Most oral ulcers are benign and self-limited, but persistent nonhealing ulcer, indurated lesion, erythroplakia/leukoplakia or neck node—especially with tobacco/alcohol or HPV risk—requires oral cancer evaluation. White plaques that scrape off suggest candidiasis.
recognize: Aphthous ulcers are painful shallow recurrent lesions; thrush often follows antibiotics, inhaled steroids, diabetes or immunosuppression.
differentiate: Oral HSV, hand-foot-mouth disease, Behçet disease and medication reactions can cause ulcerative lesions.
assessment: Ask duration, pain, trauma, tobacco/alcohol, immune status, medications, sexual/HPV risk and systemic symptoms; examine entire oral cavity and neck nodes.
workup: Biopsy persistent suspicious lesions; test for HIV, diabetes or other immunocompromise when recurrent thrush is unexplained.
management: Treat cause and refer suspicious persistent lesions promptly to dental/oral surgery/ENT.
medicationSafety: Teach mouth rinsing after inhaled corticosteroid use to reduce thrush risk.
counselling: Avoid tobacco and heavy alcohol and maintain dental care.
followUp: Document lesion resolution or biopsy referral.
examTrap: Treating a persistent indurated tongue ulcer repeatedly with topical anesthetic without biopsy referral.
oneLinePearl: An oral lesion that does not heal deserves tissue diagnosis.

title: Amenorrhea: Pregnancy First, Then Hypothalamus-Pituitary-Ovary-Outflow
bottomLine: Pregnancy is the first diagnosis to exclude in reproductive-age amenorrhea. Then classify the problem through hypothalamic, pituitary, ovarian, uterine/outflow and endocrine causes using history and targeted testing.
recognize: Weight change, intense exercise, stress, galactorrhea, hyperandrogenism, hot flashes and medication use provide diagnostic clues.
differentiate: PCOS causes chronic anovulation with hyperandrogenism; hypothalamic amenorrhea is associated with low energy availability; ovarian insufficiency causes elevated gonadotropins.
assessment: Ask pregnancy possibility, cycle history, weight/nutrition, exercise, stress, galactorrhea, headaches/vision, androgen symptoms and medications.
workup: Obtain pregnancy test, TSH and prolactin commonly, then gonadotropins/androgen studies and pelvic imaging according to phenotype.
management: Treat the cause and protect bone/endometrial health; address fertility goals without assuming pregnancy is desired.
medicationSafety: Do not start hormonal therapy simply to create withdrawal bleeding before pregnancy and serious endocrine causes are considered.
counselling: Discuss energy availability and bone health sensitively when restrictive intake or exercise contributes.
followUp: Monitor return of menses, bone risk and endocrine cause.
examTrap: Starting combined contraception for amenorrhea without first obtaining a pregnancy test.
sourceBasis: SOGC and Canadian endocrine gynecology practice resources

title: PCOS: Hyperandrogenism, Ovulatory Dysfunction, and Metabolic Risk
bottomLine: PCOS is a diagnosis of hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction with appropriate exclusion of mimics; polycystic ovarian morphology is neither necessary nor sufficient in every patient. Management addresses menstrual/endometrial protection, androgen symptoms, fertility goals and metabolic risk.
recognize: Irregular menses, hirsutism/acne and insulin resistance are common.
differentiate: Pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting tumours can mimic PCOS; rapid virilization is not typical.
assessment: Assess cycle pattern, hirsutism/acne, weight trajectory, sleep apnea, BP, diabetes risk, fertility goals, eating disorder and mood.
workup: Exclude pregnancy and key endocrine mimics; assess glycemia/lipids and use pelvic ultrasound only when diagnostically useful.
management: Use lifestyle support without stigma, hormonal cycle control/endometrial protection, antiandrogen strategies with contraception when appropriate, metformin for selected metabolic/reproductive indications and fertility therapy when desired.
medicationSafety: Antiandrogens can be teratogenic and require reliable pregnancy prevention when used.
counselling: Explain long-term diabetes and endometrial risks without implying infertility is inevitable.
followUp: Monitor cycles, metabolic risk and treatment goals.
examTrap: Diagnosing PCOS solely because an ultrasound report says 'polycystic ovaries' in a patient with regular cycles and no hyperandrogenism.
oneLinePearl: PCOS is a clinical-endocrine syndrome, not an ultrasound appearance.
sourceBasis: SOGC and international evidence adapted to Canadian practice

title: Dysmenorrhea: Primary Pain or Secondary Pelvic Disease?
bottomLine: Primary dysmenorrhea begins around menses without pelvic pathology and responds to NSAIDs or hormonal suppression. Progressive pain, dyspareunia, abnormal bleeding, infertility or poor response should raise endometriosis, adenomyosis or other secondary causes.
recognize: Primary dysmenorrhea often begins within a few years of menarche and is crampy lower abdominal pain around menstruation.
differentiate: Endometriosis can begin in adolescence and should not be dismissed because the patient is young.
assessment: Ask timing, severity, school/work absence, sexual symptoms, bleeding, bowel/bladder symptoms and medication response.
workup: No routine imaging is required for classic primary dysmenorrhea; pelvic ultrasound and referral are used when secondary disease is suspected.
management: Use correctly timed NSAIDs and/or hormonal suppression; escalate persistent disabling symptoms for endometriosis evaluation.
medicationSafety: NSAID GI/renal risks and estrogen contraindications should be reviewed.
counselling: Validate menstrual pain and functional impact; severe pain is not something patients must simply tolerate.
followUp: Reassess after an adequate therapeutic trial rather than repeating the same ineffective plan indefinitely.
examTrap: Telling an adolescent with disabling progressive menstrual pain that endometriosis cannot occur until adulthood.
oneLinePearl: Age does not protect against endometriosis.
sourceBasis: SOGC endometriosis and dysmenorrhea practice resources

title: Fatigue: Sleep, Mood, Blood, Thyroid, Medications, Systemic Disease
bottomLine: Fatigue is a symptom, not a laboratory panel. Use duration, sleepiness versus low energy, mood, medications, bleeding, infection, endocrine and systemic clues to build a targeted differential before ordering tests.
recognize: Sleep deprivation/OSA, depression/anxiety, anemia, thyroid disease, pregnancy, medications and chronic inflammatory disease are common causes.
differentiate: Excessive daytime sleepiness points toward sleep disorders; exertional dyspnea may represent cardiopulmonary disease rather than generic fatigue.
assessment: Ask sleep quality/duration, snoring, mood, weight, fever, bleeding, diet, medications/substances, pregnancy, pain and functional change.
workup: Use targeted CBC, ferritin, TSH, pregnancy or other tests based on history; broad autoimmune, vitamin or imaging panels are low value without clues.
management: Treat identified cause and address sleep, activity, mental health and social strain while avoiding unsupported supplement prescribing.
medicationSafety: Sedatives, antihistamines, gabapentinoids and polypharmacy commonly cause fatigue.
counselling: Set expectations that diagnosis may emerge through focused follow-up rather than one giant test battery.
followUp: Reassess persistent unexplained fatigue for evolving red flags.
examTrap: Ordering an extensive autoimmune and vitamin panel for two weeks of fatigue in a patient sleeping four hours nightly without first addressing sleep.
oneLinePearl: Fatigue workup starts with the story of energy and sleep.
sourceBasis: Canadian primary care diagnostic stewardship principles

title: Unintentional Weight Loss: Malignancy, GI, Endocrine, Mood, or Access?
bottomLine: Unintentional weight loss is a clinically important symptom at any starting body size. Confirm the trajectory and investigate malignancy, GI disease, endocrine disease, infection, depression, medications and food insecurity from the accompanying clues.
recognize: Older adults may lose weight from dentition, swallowing, dementia, social isolation and medications as well as cancer.
differentiate: Intentional weight loss should still be assessed for unsafe methods or eating disorders when the rate or context is concerning.
assessment: Confirm prior weights and appetite, GI symptoms, fever/night sweats, pain, dental/swallowing, depression, substances, medications, food access and cancer screening.
workup: Use CBC, chemistry, liver, thyroid and age/risk-directed cancer or GI evaluation based on the presentation; avoid indiscriminate whole-body imaging as first step without clinical direction.
management: Treat the cause, address nutrition and food access and escalate concerning cancer or systemic disease features promptly.
medicationSafety: Medication adverse effects and overtreated diabetes/thyroid disease can contribute.
counselling: Do not congratulate unintended loss because the patient had a higher BMI.
followUp: Reweigh and reassess until the trajectory stabilizes or cause is established.
examTrap: Congratulating a patient with obesity on major unintentional weight loss and missing colon cancer symptoms.
oneLinePearl: Unintentional weight loss is a symptom at every body size.
sourceBasis: Canadian primary care and geriatrics practice principles

title: Edema: Heart, Kidney, Liver, Vein, Drug, or Lymph?
bottomLine: Bilateral edema is a physiology problem, not a diagnosis. Determine whether volume overload, venous disease, low oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction or medication effect is driving it before prescribing more diuretic.
recognize: Heart failure adds dyspnea/JVP; nephrotic disease adds proteinuria/hypoalbuminemia; cirrhosis adds portal/liver features; venous edema worsens with dependency.
differentiate: Unilateral acute swelling raises DVT or local obstruction/infection; lymphedema is often nonpitting later and may involve skin thickening.
assessment: Assess dyspnea/orthopnea, JVP, weight trend, urine, liver disease, venous symptoms, medications such as DHP CCBs/NSAIDs and pregnancy.
workup: Use BNP/echo, urinalysis/ACR, renal/liver tests or venous imaging according to the pattern.
management: Treat the cause; use compression for appropriate venous disease after arterial risk consideration and diuretics for true volume overload rather than medication-related capillary edema.
medicationSafety: DHP calcium-channel blocker edema often does not respond well to simply adding a loop diuretic and can create a prescribing cascade.
counselling: Track weight and symptoms when volume status is being actively treated.
followUp: Reassess edema after changing a suspected culprit medication.
examTrap: Adding furosemide to amlodipine-related ankle edema without reconsidering the amlodipine.
oneLinePearl: Not all edema is excess total-body fluid.
sourceBasis: Canadian cardiovascular, renal and primary care practice principles

title: Common Cold and Acute Cough: Safety-Net Without Antibiotics
bottomLine: Most acute upper-respiratory infections and uncomplicated acute bronchitis are viral and improve without antibiotics. The NP's job is to identify pneumonia, asthma/COPD, pertussis, severe infection or other red flags while treating symptoms and giving a credible expected course.
recognize: Cough can last weeks after a viral infection; coloured sputum alone does not identify bacterial disease.
differentiate: Abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings, hypoxemia or significant dyspnea increase pneumonia probability; prolonged paroxysmal cough can suggest pertussis.
assessment: Assess duration, fever, dyspnea, chest pain, oxygenation when warranted, comorbidity, immune status, smoking/vaping and outbreak exposure.
workup: No routine chest x-ray, viral panel or blood testing for uncomplicated low-risk URI/bronchitis; test when the result changes antiviral, infection-control or diagnostic management.
management: Use hydration, analgesia and targeted symptom strategies; avoid antibiotics for uncomplicated viral disease and treat confirmed/suspected high-consequence infections appropriately.
medicationSafety: OTC cough/cold products have pediatric and cardiovascular risks; decongestants can worsen hypertension and palpitations.
counselling: Give expected cough duration so patients know persistence does not automatically mean antibiotic failure.
followUp: Reassess worsening or failure to improve beyond the expected course.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics because sputum became green during acute bronchitis.
oneLinePearl: Green sputum is an inflammation clue, not an antibiotic indication.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Cold Standard and antimicrobial stewardship resources
